title: The Effects of Extended Unemployment Insurance over the Business Cycle
research_question: How does extending the potential duration of unemployment insurance benefits affect nonemployment duration, actual benefit duration, and benefit exhaustion rates, and how do these effects vary between booms and recessions? In particular, does the disincentive (moral hazard) cost of longer UI entitlements change systematically with labor market conditions relative to the additional insurance coverage UI extensions provide?
data_description: The study uses the universe of German social security administrative records covering every employment spell in social-security-covered jobs and every unemployment insurance spell from 1975 to 2008, with day-to-day longitudinal precision. Key variables include exact age at UI claim, daily wages, UI benefit levels and durations, nonemployment duration (time from UI claim to next registered employment, capped at 36 months), job tenure, industry, occupation, education, gender, nationality, and employer characteristics. The unit of observation is an individual unemployment spell. The analysis sample consists of UI spells starting between July 1987 and December 2004 for workers aged 40–49, focusing primarily on those with strong prior labor force attachment (at least 52 months of employment in the previous 7 years without intermittent UI), yielding roughly two million spells. Macroeconomic indicators (GDP growth, national/industry unemployment rates, mass-layoff rates, industry wage losses) are merged in to characterize cyclical conditions.
institutional_context: Germany's unemployment insurance system replaces about 63% of prior net earnings (68% with children) for workers who lose jobs without fault and have worked at least 12 of the previous 36 months. Crucially, the maximum potential duration of UI benefits depends on the claimant's exact age at the start of the spell and prior employment history, with sharp jumps at specific age thresholds. Between July 1987 and March 1999, eligible workers received 12 months below age 42, 18 months from age 42, 22 months from age 44, and 26 months from age 49. A 1999 reform shifted these thresholds upward by three years (e.g., to ages 45 and 47). After UI exhaustion, means-tested unemployment assistance (UA) is available, though spousal income substantially reduces UA receipt. These age-based potential durations remained invariant to business cycle conditions throughout the sample period, unlike countercyclical UI extensions used in countries such as the United States, providing stable policy variation across recessions and booms including German reunification and the subsequent slump.
ground_truth_notes: LLM extraction focused on secondary finding (moral hazard declining in recessions). Main treatment effect (UI→longer unemployment) is positive. Manually corrected.
